summary:
ARES: The Last 30 Sols is a browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to run a Mars outpost. It was built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”.

The player is the mission commander of a four-person crew. Across six levels they learn the five systems the challenge names: life support, power, food production, radiation shielding and communication delay. Each level has three star goals and a badge, and the last level combines everything in a 30-Sol survival mission on an outpost the child builds.

Play happens inside a 3D outpost. The child walks the base, talks to crew specialists, and answers a decision on each Sol, where every choice helps one system and costs another. In Level 1 the oxygen repair switches to a first-person view: the child scans the machine for a leak, then fixes it with tools.

The science uses real NASA figures, such as Curiosity’s radiation reading of 0.64 mSv per day on Mars and 0.84 kg of oxygen per astronaut per day. Every number is tagged as a NASA observation or a simplified game value.

The aim is that after ten minutes of play, a child can explain how astronauts stay alive on Mars.
details:
ARES: The Last 30 Sols is a browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to run a Mars outpost. The player is the commander of a four-person crew and plays through six levels. Each of the first five levels teaches one mission system: life support, power, food production, radiation shielding and communication delay. The sixth level combines them in a 30-Sol survival mission on an outpost the child builds with limited rocket cargo. Inside a 3D outpost, the child walks the base, talks to crew specialists and solves tasks at the machines before the Sol timer ends. Each Sol brings a decision where helping one system costs another, and the game then explains what happened and why. In Level 1 the oxygen repair switches to a first-person view: the child scans three joints with a leak detector, then isolates the leak, replaces the seal, sets the pressure and tests it.

The main benefit is that children learn by doing, with short text, large visuals and a read-aloud button for younger players. The outpost shows its own problems through warning lights, dusty solar panels and wilting plants, so the child can see what is wrong without reading a chart. Each level has three star goals and a badge, which makes progress clear. The game runs in a browser with no installation, so a school can use it on the computers it already has.

Our intended impact is that after ten minutes of play, a child can explain how astronauts stay alive on Mars. Beyond the facts, the game teaches trade-off thinking: every good choice has a cost somewhere else, which is how real mission engineers work.

We built the project with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step. We used Three.js for the 3D outpost, the crew and the first-person view, and the browser’s own audio and speech features for sound effects and read-aloud. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages. The science is based on NASA sources: Curiosity RAD radiation measurements, NASA life support design values, the Space Station water recovery milestone, NASA Mars facts, and the DONKI, OSDR RadLab and Mars Trek resources. We used the AI tools Claude and ChatGPT to assist with design, code generation and testing.

The project is creative because the child lives inside the outpost instead of reading a dashboard or answering a quiz. They repair a machine with their own hands in first person, and the leak is in a different place each time, so it cannot be memorised. Decisions ripple across systems, so the child feels how connected a mission is.

Our team considered four main factors. The first was age: after feedback from the committee, we replaced a professional dashboard with a game a 7-year-old can play. The second was honesty: every number is tagged as a NASA observation or a simplified game value, with sources listed in the Science Lab. The third was reliability: the game falls back to saved NASA data when there is no internet at the venue. The fourth was tone: a failed mission ends with the crew flying home safely, so children are encouraged to try again.
